passage: "Saurabh, I went back to our old flat in Kolkata last week. Just stood outside. The building's been painted this weird green. The mango tree where we tied the cricket stumps is gone. And the tea stall uncle still recognised me! He said, 'Arnab babu, you've grown a beard.' I laughed and then had to turn away because my eyes were stinging. I kept thinking of summers when the only worry was whose turn it was to bat. Now it's rent, exams, job forms, Ma's health. Part of me wants to go back to being that nine-year-old, just for a day. But then I remember I also hated being told what to do all the time. It's weird. I miss it, and I'm glad it's over."

qa.q: What had happened to the mango tree outside Arnab's old flat?
qa.a: It was gone.

qa.q: Why did Arnab have to turn away at the tea stall?
qa.a: Being recognised brought back memories of his carefree childhood, and he felt a sudden rush of longing that made his eyes sting.

qa.q: What could Arnab do with this feeling instead of just aching?
qa.a: He could share memories with old friends like Saurabh or make small time for play, letting nostalgia comfort him without pulling him backward.

qa.q: How might the tea stall uncle have felt seeing Arnab again?
qa.a: He was probably happy and a bit amazed at how the boy had grown up, remembering him as a child in the lane.

grounding: A young man describes a bittersweet longing for the simple safety of his childhood while facing adult worries.

passage: During exam week, my roommate Aditi started doing strange things. I'm Pankaj, we share a study room in our college flat, and she's usually all planners and highlighters. But on Tuesday night I found her watching old cartoons we both grew up with, the theme song on repeat, eating the cheap orange candy we used to buy for one rupee. She'd found a packet at a shop near the station. When I teased her, she laughed and said, "Everything was simpler when this was my biggest problem." She said it lightly, but she didn't look at me. Later I saw her looking at a photo of her grandmother's house on her phone. I can't say for sure what she's feeling. Maybe it's the exams. Maybe she just misses being small.

qa.q: Where did Aditi find the orange candy?
qa.a: At a shop near the station.

qa.q: What does Aditi's comment about things being simpler suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems to be longing for the safety of childhood as a comfort against exam stress, though she says it lightly.

qa.q: How could Pankaj support Aditi without prying?
qa.a: Pankaj could join her for an episode, share some childhood memories of their own, and gently ask how she is coping with exams.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Aditi's change during exam week?
qa.a: Pankaj is surprised, since she is usually organised, and admits being unable to be sure what she's feeling.

grounding: A roommate describes a young adult seeking comfort in childhood memories and treats during stressful exams.

passage:
Before: The week before her family sold their old house, Ayesha, twenty, packed up her childhood room. She found her Class 4 diary under the bed: "Today Varun and I made a tent from bedsheets. Best day ever." She laughed, then sat on the floor for a long time.

During: On moving day she argued with Ammi about keeping a broken toy piano. "It's junk, Ayesha." "It's mine." She won. It went into the car, wrapped in a towel.

After: A month later in her college hostel, she pinned a photo of the old gate above her bed. She video-called Varun, now at university in another city. "Remember the bedsheet tent?" He groaned. "You're so dramatic." But he stayed on the call for an hour, talking about old summers.

qa.q: What did Ayesha and Varun make from bedsheets in Class 4?
qa.a: A tent.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha fight to keep the broken toy piano?
qa.a: It held memories of her childhood home, and letting it go felt like losing part of that safe, simpler time.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha carry her nostalgia into her new life in a healthy way?
qa.a: Pinning the photo and calling Varun let her keep the memories close and share them, instead of just grieving alone.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on the call, despite teasing her?
qa.a: He probably misses those summers too, since he stays on for an hour talking about them. 😊

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood as the family home is sold.

passage: 'Pooja, you asked why I keep driving past that old school,' said Samir, the senior engineer, as they waited at the signal. 'When I was twenty-one, in my final year, I went back there on a holiday. The guard let me in. The benches were so small. I sat on one and smelled chalk and the wet mud of the field, and suddenly I wanted to be ten again so badly it hurt. Back then someone packed my tiffin, someone else decided everything. I didn't have to choose a job or worry about my father's loan. I sat there for an hour. Then I walked out feeling strangely lighter. It was sweet and sad together. I still visit when life gets heavy.'

qa.q: What could young Samir smell sitting on the bench?
qa.a: Chalk and the wet mud of the field.

qa.q: What did Samir wish for while sitting on the small bench?
qa.a: Samir longed for the safety of being ten, when others made decisions and there were no adult worries.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make at twenty-one on that holiday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Samir chose to go back to the old school and sit with the longing for an hour instead of pushing it away; feeling it fully let Samir walk out lighter.

qa.q: How might the guard have seen a grown former student sitting on a child's bench for an hour?
qa.a: The guard may have been puzzled at first, or quietly touched, watching someone come back to sit so long in a place meant for small children.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for the simplicity and safety of childhood, told as a memory by a senior engineer.

passage: The truck was coming at six the next morning, and the old house in Bhopal had to be empty by then. Imran, nineteen, home from his hostel for just one day, was supposed to pack the storeroom. Rain drummed on the tin roof; the power kept flickering. He opened a trunk and found his old cricket bat, taped at the handle, with his name scratched in by Abba's knife. He sat down on the dusty floor holding it. His sister Swati found him there an hour later, nothing packed. 'Imran! We don't have time.' 'Remember when this whole yard was the world?' he said. She stopped. Then she sat beside him, just for five minutes, and neither of them spoke. After that they packed fast, and he put the bat in his own bag.

qa.q: When was the truck coming?
qa.a: At six the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Imran sit on the floor holding the bat instead of packing?
qa.a: It brought back the safe, simple world of his childhood in that house, and he felt a bittersweet longing he couldn't rush past.

qa.q: What did Swati get right despite the time pressure?
qa.a: She paused and sat with him briefly, honouring the feeling, and then they packed quickly together.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when she first found him with nothing packed?
qa.a: Frustrated and stressed about the deadline, until his words pulled her into the memory too.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood while emptying the family home against a deadline.
